why: One property here has no off-the-shelf equivalent and one does, so defending both as bespoke would be a rubber stamp. The unique property is cross_check (run.py:237-277): for every prompt a skill's own fixture says must route to it, score that prompt against EVERY OTHER description in the corpus -- including skills that ship no fixture -- and fail when a rival ties or beats the owner. Every skill linter found (himself65/skill-lint, swarmclawai/agent-skills-lint) validates one SKILL.md in isolation against the agentskills.io schema; agent-skills-lint's `collisions` command was checked and it finds duplicate NAMES, not overlapping descriptions. promptfoo's Test Agent Skills guide has `not-skill-used`, but that is a hand-authored negative you write per pair after you already suspect the conflict -- it discovers nothing. Paired with that: UNCOVERED as a counted first-class state and the NOTHING-GRADED guard (run.py:331-338), which makes a green on zero graded skills unreachable, and the fixture-integrity rules (run.py:199-210) that reject an all-positive suite as unfalsifiable -- these are the exact defect the tool was written against and no alternative checks them. But the SPLIT is real in two places. First, the structural half (run.py:86-126 hand-rolled non-YAML frontmatter parser, plus run.py:153-169 name/description/emoji checks) is strictly weaker than himself65/skill-lint, which additionally enforces the 1-1024 char description bound, an allowed-fields whitelist, body line limits, and reference-file existence; ours explicitly is not a YAML parser and leaves anything structured as raw text. Second and more important: run.py:12-24 admits in its own docstring that this measures a lower bound and does not simulate model routing -- and the thing it is a proxy for is shipped, maintained and off the shelf as promptfoo's `skill-used` assertion. The honest position is that the lexical grader is a zero-cost CI pre-filter that should stay, the structural checks should defer to a spec linter if a Node dependency is ever acceptable, and a real behavioural oracle is missing from this repo and should be adopted rather than approximated forever.

alternatives.name: promptfoo -- Test Agent Skills guide and the `skill-used` assertion (promptfoo.dev/docs/guides/test-agent-skills/, OSS, promptfoo/promptfoo)
alternatives.covers: The measurement this component explicitly declines to make. Fetched the guide 2026-07-29: it normalises provider tool calls into a `skill-used` signal so a routing assertion works without provider-specific heuristics, supports `not-skill-used` for negative boundaries, and compares skill versions on invocation, task quality, cost and latency. This is the real oracle for 'did the model actually route here', for which anchor_score is only a proxy.
alternatives.gap: Confirmed from the same fetch: it performs NO static or lexical analysis of description text without a model call, has NO cross-skill collision discovery (you must hand-author each `not-skill-used` pair, so it can only confirm a conflict you already guessed), and does NOT report skills that carry no fixture at all -- so it cannot produce the 42-uncovered census this repo's scan printed on 2026-07-29. It also cannot run in a no-API-key, no-network CI step, which is the constraint that made this tool stdlib-only.
alternatives.cost: npx/npm (Node runtime added to a Python-stdlib-only repo) plus a real provider API key and per-run token spend for every case, every run. Free/OSS licence; exact SPDX not verified this session.
alternatives.maturity: Actively maintained: 2026-dated third-party guides and reviews found in search, and the agent-skills guide itself is current documentation. Release cadence and star count NOT independently verified -- I did not run `gh release list`.

alternatives.name: adewale/skill-eval-harness (GitHub, PyPI `skill-eval-harness`, MIT)
alternatives.covers: The closest whole-shape competitor found. Per its README fetched 2026-07-29: per-skill `evals/shared-benchmark.json` manifests with id/split/prompt/files/expected_behavior/assertions, a paired with-skill vs without-skill design to measure causal lift, `audit-manifest` for a readiness verdict, and leakage lint for prompt-answer overlap. Grading and aggregation run deterministically offline; only the generation phases touch a model.
alternatives.gap: Its offline half grades RUN OUTPUT, not description text -- generation (`run-claude`/`run-codex`/`run-agent`) still requires model calls, so nothing in it produces a verdict from two strings alone. README shows no cross-skill collision detection and no explicit uncovered-skill reporting; it is case-level pass-rate oriented. Its leakage lint measures prompt-vs-answer overlap, which is a different quantity from prompt-vs-sibling-description overlap. Its fixture schema is also incompatible with the three names this tool reads (run.py:44).
alternatives.cost: `uv tool install skill-eval-harness` -- a real PyPI dependency plus model spend for the generation phases. MIT.
alternatives.maturity: README showed 59 stars and 98 commits on main with a CHANGELOG and pinned releases (0.6.0 cited as the pin example). I did NOT verify last-commit date or whether releases are recent.

alternatives.name: himself65/skill-lint (GitHub, npm `skill-lint`, MIT)
alternatives.covers: Strictly supersedes the structural half of grade() (run.py:153-169) and would let the hand-rolled frontmatter parser (run.py:86-126) be deleted. Verified rule list from its README: real YAML frontmatter validation, required name/description, name format (1-64 chars, [a-z0-9-], no leading/trailing/consecutive hyphens), name-vs-directory consistency, description length 1-1024, allowed-fields-only whitelist, body under ~500 lines / ~5000 tokens, reference depth and referenced-file existence, plus opt-in Claude.ai checks for reserved words and angle brackets.
alternatives.gap: Its README was checked specifically for this and it does NOT do test-prompt routing or trigger evaluation, description-to-prompt scoring, or cross-skill collision detection. So it replaces roughly 60 lines of this component and touches none of anchor_score, the separation check, fixture integrity, cross_check, UNCOVERED accounting, or the NOTHING-GRADED guard. It also has no concept of the repo's own no-emoji rule beyond the Claude.ai angle-bracket check.
alternatives.cost: Node runtime + `npx skill-lint` or a global npm install, in a repo whose whole gate story is stdlib-only Python running offline on Windows. MIT. This dependency cost is the single reason the structural half is not an unconditional adopt.
alternatives.maturity: MIT and available as CLI and GitHub Action per README. Maintenance status NOT verified -- no commit or release dates were visible on the page fetched, and I did not query the API for them.

alternatives.name: swarmclawai/agent-skills-lint (GitHub, MIT)
alternatives.covers: Cross-agent frontmatter schema validation (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Aider and others) with a core name+description schema plus per-agent extensions, safe installation, and an index of what is installed.
alternatives.gap: Checked directly because 'collision-aware' in its description sounded like this component's cross_check: it is NOT. Its `collisions` command finds skills with DUPLICATE NAMES silently overriding each other. It has no test-prompt execution, no description-versus-prompt scoring, and no description-overlap detection. Two skills named differently whose descriptions subsume each other -- the live gws-gmail / gws-gmail-read case this component was built around (run.py:237-254) -- are invisible to it.

alternatives.maturity: WEAK and I am saying so rather than rounding up: the page showed 4 stars and a single commit on main, with CI present. Not a dependency I would put in a gate on that evidence.

alternatives.name: Anthropic's own plugin-dev `skill-development` skill and `skill-reviewer` agent (anthropics/claude-code, plugins/plugin-dev)
alternatives.covers: First-party guidance on description quality: third person, specific trigger phrases, concrete scenarios, not vague. This is the authoritative statement of what a good routing surface looks like, and it is the standard this component is mechanising.
alternatives.gap: Fetched the SKILL.md 2026-07-29 and it ships NO executable validator, NO eval runner, NO routing/trigger test, and NO description-overlap check. Step 5 'Validate and Test' is a human checklist plus 'ask the skill-reviewer agent to review my skill' -- i.e. a model reading one skill in prose. Nothing in it is runnable in CI, nothing produces an exit code, and nothing sees two skills at once.
alternatives.cost: Zero install (bundled), but a model call per review and a non-deterministic, non-reproducible verdict.
alternatives.maturity: First-party and current on main as of the fetch. I did NOT check whether a newer first-party validator exists outside this file.

alternatives.name: Rasa Open Source -- `rasa test nlu` intent confusion matrix and cross-validation (rasa.com docs / legacy-docs-oss.rasa.com)
alternatives.covers: The classical, pre-LLM form of exactly the problem cross_check attacks. Produces intent_report.json, intent_confusion_matrix.png and a confidence histogram showing which intents get mistaken for which, plus cross-validation for when you split one intent into two, plus errors.json listing every misprediction. Forum threads confirm 'different intents contain the same words in a similar order' is the recognised failure and merging-plus-slots the recognised fix.
alternatives.gap: It measures a TRAINED CLASSIFIER over many labelled utterances per intent; it cannot evaluate a single natural-language description string, which is the entire routing surface here. Adopting it means inventing training data this repo does not have (today: 5 fixtures, 42 uncovered skills, and fixtures of 4-5 cases each -- nowhere near a trainable set), running a training pipeline, and accepting heavy ML dependencies. It also has no notion of SKILL.md structure, frontmatter, or an uncovered census.
alternatives.cost: Large Python ML stack and a training step, for a repo whose stated requirement is a no-network no-model check reproducible from two strings (run.py:22-24).
alternatives.maturity: Long-established and documented; 2024-2026 forum and docs pages surfaced. Current release status NOT verified.

alternatives.name: ranx / pytrec_eval / ir-measures (Python ranking-evaluation libraries; ranx published at ECIR 2022, ir-measur.es)
alternatives.covers: The arithmetic half of cross_check done properly. cross_check is precision@1 over a corpus of 47 descriptions with an ad-hoc tie rule; these libraries compute Precision, MRR, MAP, nDCG and Hit Rate from qrels + runs, and ranx documents that its metrics are tested against trec_eval for correctness. Adopting one would give principled tie handling, per-query breakdowns and statistical comparison between two versions of the description corpus.
alternatives.gap: They evaluate a ranking you already produced -- they do not read SKILL.md, do not parse frontmatter, do not score text against text, do not know what a fixture is, and have no PASS/FAIL/UNCOVERED verdict or exit code. You would still write the scorer, the corpus loader, the fixture reader and the verdict logic; only ~40 lines of run.py:258-277 would move. ranx also pulls numba/numpy, which is a heavy dependency for that trade.
alternatives.cost: pip dependencies (ranx: numba+numpy; pytrec_eval: a C extension needing a compiler on Windows) in a currently zero-dependency stdlib tool.
alternatives.maturity: ranx is peer-reviewed (ECIR 2022) and on PyPI; ir-measures documents eight providers including trec_eval bindings. Current maintenance cadence NOT verified this session.

alternatives.name: rank_bm25 / bm25s / scikit-learn TfidfVectorizer (lexical scoring libraries)
alternatives.covers: A better-calibrated replacement for anchor_score (run.py:73-83), which is a raw unweighted overlap ratio. IDF weighting would stop the shared token 'gmail' -- present in four sibling descriptions in this tree -- from carrying the same weight as a discriminating token, which is precisely the signal cross_check is hunting for. bm25s is documented as depending only on numpy/scipy.
alternatives.gap: A scoring function is not the component. It supplies no fixture format, no frontmatter reading, no separation rule, no all-positive-fixture rejection, no uncovered census, no exit code. It would also break a deliberate design property stated at run.py:503-508: no stemming, so that any failure is readable back to the two exact strings that caused it -- an IDF score computed over a 47-document corpus is not reconstructible by a human staring at one description. Search results also note the standard caveat that lexical scoring misses paraphrase entirely, which is a limitation ours already inherits.
alternatives.cost: numpy/scipy (bm25s) or pure-Python (rank_bm25) or the full scikit-learn stack. All add a dependency to a tool that currently imports argparse/json/os/re/sys/tempfile only.
alternatives.maturity: rank_bm25 and bm25s both have public GitHub repos; BM25S has a 2024 arXiv paper. Neither's current maintenance state was verified.

alternatives.name: DeepEval ToolCorrectnessMetric (deepeval.com, Confident AI, OSS Python)
alternatives.covers: pytest-native agent evaluation with a ToolCorrectnessMetric that compares tools actually called against an expected-tools list, with configurable strictness (name only, or arguments/output too), plus ArgumentCorrectnessMetric. If skills were modelled as tools, this is the CI-shaped assertion for 'did it pick the right one'.
alternatives.gap: It grades an agent TRACE -- it needs a real run that produced tool calls, so it cannot answer anything from a SKILL.md alone. No frontmatter validation, no description-overlap analysis, no uncovered-skill census, and no notion of Claude Code's skill format. Also 50+ of its metrics are LLM-judged, which reintroduces model cost and non-determinism into a check that currently costs nothing.
alternatives.cost: pip install deepeval plus model spend for the run being traced and for any judged metric.
alternatives.maturity: Actively promoted with 2026-dated comparison pages from its vendor (Confident AI), so treat maturity claims as partly vendor-sourced. Independent release cadence NOT verified.

alternatives.name: MetaTool / ToolE benchmark (arXiv 2310.03128, OpenReview R0c2qtalgG)
alternatives.covers: The academic framing of this exact problem: 21,000+ prompts with ground-truth tool assignments, and a named subtask 'tool selection with similar choices' that is the research version of cross_check. Directly relevant finding for this component: the authors had to manually eliminate tools whose descriptions were too brief or unclear for the model to understand, and they recommend rewriting descriptions per downstream model -- i.e. the literature agrees description quality is the causal variable.
alternatives.gap: It is a benchmark for scoring MODELS, not a runnable linter for YOUR skill library. It ships no tool that reads your descriptions, no CI integration, no exit code, and its overlap handling is a dataset-construction step (merging and decomposing tools) rather than a detector you can point at 47 local SKILL.md files.
alternatives.cost: None to read; adopting its methodology means model inference over thousands of prompts.
alternatives.maturity: Published and peer-reviewed with multiple arXiv versions (v5 seen). Whether the ToolE dataset or code is still maintained was NOT verified.

what_ours_does: run.py (578 lines, one file, stdlib-only: argparse/json/os/re/sys/tempfile) grades every skill directory under a root and exits nonzero on a defect. `scan` (run.py:280-341) walks the root and calls grade() per directory; `selftest` (run.py:355-554) is the regression suite. grade() (run.py:143-234) does four things. STRUCTURE (run.py:153-169): reads the SKILL.md frontmatter with a deliberately hand-rolled non-YAML parser (run.py:86-126, which does handle `description: >-` folded block scalars because dot-claude/skills/ship-gate uses one and treating it as empty produced a false 'missing description' report), then flags a missing frontmatter block, a missing name, a name that disagrees with the directory, an empty description ('nothing can route to it'), and any emoji in the description per the repo's no-emoji rule (EMOJI_RX, run.py:49-51). FIXTURE INTEGRITY (run.py:171-210): loads the first of routing-evals.json / evals.json / trigger-evals.json that exists (run.py:44, 129-140); a file that exists but will not parse is reported as its own distinct failure rather than folded into a malformed-case count, because the wrong diagnosis sends someone to the wrong line (run.py:185-190); cases missing a non-empty `prompt` or an `expect` of exactly trigger|skip are counted and named; a fixture with no `skip` case fails as unfalsifiable and one with no `trigger` case fails as unreachable (run.py:207-210) -- this is the imported defect the tool exists for. SEPARATION (run.py:214-230): anchor_score (run.py:73-83) is the fraction of a prompt's content words that the description also uses, normalised by the PROMPT so a long description cannot win by covering more vocabulary; the check compares the WEAKEST trigger prompt against the STRONGEST skip prompt and fails if the skip wins or ties, and separately fails any trigger prompt scoring exactly 0.0 as unroutable by text. No stemming, deliberately (rationale at run.py:503-508: stemming would compress every score toward every other and make failures unreadable back to the two strings). CROSS-SKILL (run.py:237-277): scores each trigger prompt against every other description in the corpus, including skills with no fixture of their own, since a rival needs no fixture to steal a prompt; a rival that strictly outranks the owner is OUTRANKED and fatal, an exact tie is reported as a weak signal and only fatal under --strict-ties, with the arithmetic reason given inline (small-denominator ratios collide often). There is deliberately no per-case opt-out. VERDICT ACCOUNTING (run.py:287-341): PASS/FAIL/UNCOVERED matches tools/gate/gate.py's vocabulary; an uncovered skill is printed and named, never silently skipped; --strict makes uncovered fatal; and run.py:331-338 makes a green over zero graded skills impossible ('NOTHING GRADED'), a guard added after the first real run against this tree printed 'PASS on 0 graded skill(s)'. selftest (run.py:355-554) is planted-fault-plus-clean-twin throughout: an inverted fixture, an anchorless trigger, a well-worded trigger sitting beside a badly-worded one (added because every earlier faulted fixture had exactly one trigger, so weakest and strongest were the same case and sorting the wrong way was invisible), all-positive and all-negative fixtures, a bad expect value, a name/directory mismatch, an emoji, an empty description, a missing fixture, an unparseable fixture, a folded block scalar, a parent description that subsumes a child, a tie that must stay green by default and go red under --strict-ties, and a tree where nothing has a fixture. Several of these are annotated as having been found by mutation testing rather than by design. Its failure marker is literally `[FAIL]` because tools/audit/mutate.py parses that prefix to attribute a caught mutation to a named check (run.py:373-378).
strongest_counterargument: The lexical grader may be measuring nothing that matters, and the live numbers are consistent with that. anchor_score is unweighted set-overlap over content words. Real routing is a model reading descriptions, and the tool's own docstring concedes it does not simulate that (run.py:12-24) -- so a PASS here is compatible with the model routing every one of those prompts wrong, and a FAIL is compatible with the model routing them all correctly. It is a lower bound whose tightness has never been measured against actual routing behaviour, and this record found no evidence anyone has established that such a bound correlates with model selection. Meanwhile the empirical yield on this tree is thin: 47 skills, 5 with fixtures, 0 fail, 0 outranked, and the single finding is a 0.40/0.40 tie between gws-gmail and explain-simply which the tool itself classifies as weak signal and refuses to fail on. The one collision the docstring cites as the motivating case, gws-gmail subsuming gws-gmail-read, does not appear in the current scan at all -- all three gws skills now PASS with healthy margins, so the live tree provides no confirmed instance of the unique property firing in anger. 578 lines of which roughly 200 are selftest, producing one non-fatal tie, is a poor ratio; a defender should notice that most of the file's density is in comments explaining bugs found in the tool itself rather than defects found in the skills. The stronger construction of the counterargument is that this is inverted: the repo spent its effort on a cheap proxy because the real oracle costs money, when promptfoo's `skill-used` plus one afternoon of fixtures would produce an actual routing measurement, and the correct verdict might be a full 'adopt' -- run promptfoo on a small, cheap, occasionally-refreshed suite, delete the lexical scorer, and keep only the ~80 lines of uncovered census and fixture-integrity rules that no one else ships. The defence rests on 'it costs nothing and runs offline', which is an argument about price, not about validity, and price is not evidence.
